resolved_by: Guidelines amendment effective November 1992, which changed U.S.S.G. § 3E1.1(a) to require acceptance 'for his offense' and clarified that a defendant need not admit uncharged criminal conduct to earn the reduction
issue: May a sentencing court deny the acceptance-of-responsibility reduction because the defendant denied uncharged relevant conduct, without violating the Fifth Amendment?

sides.position: The court may consider the defendant's denial of relevant conduct in deciding whether to grant the acceptance-of-responsibility reduction.
cases: United States v. Frierson, 945 F.2d 650 (3d Cir. 1991)
United States v. Gordon, 895 F.2d 932 (4th Cir. 1990)
United States v. Mourning, 914 F.2d 699 (5th Cir. 1990)
United States v. Munio, 909 F.2d 436 (11th Cir. 1990)
United States v. Lemaine, No. 24-14049 (11th Cir. 2026)

sides.position: Conditioning the reduction on an admission of relevant conduct would violate the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination, so the guideline is read to avoid that problem.
cases: United States v. Perez-Franco, 873 F.2d 455 (1st Cir. 1989)
United States v. Oliveras, 905 F.2d 623 (2d Cir. 1990)
United States v. Piper, 918 F.2d 839 (9th Cir. 1990)

quote: As Lemaine acknowledges, this last change was to clarify only that a defendant need not admit to uncharged criminal conduct to earn the reduction because a circuit split had developed over whether such a requirement would violate the Fifth Amendment.
cite: United States v. Chadwick Lemaine, No. 24-14049 (11th Cir. 2026)
